  • Black or dark brown vaginal discharge: what to check
Family Health

Black or dark brown vaginal discharge: what to check

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Blood can darken as it takes longer to leave the uterus or vagina. A small amount mixed with discharge may look deep brown or almost black, especially near the end of a period. Colour alone, however, cannot tell you whether the cause is harmless, an infection or a pregnancy-related problem.

Consider the whole pattern

If a little dark discharge occurs at the end of your usual period and then stops, without pain, unpleasant odour or other new symptoms, it may simply be older menstrual blood. It does not mean you need to cleanse the vagina or “flush out” retained blood.

Seek assessment for a new or persistent change, bleeding between periods or after sex, unusually heavy or prolonged bleeding, or discharge with itching, pain or an unpleasant smell. A photograph or colour chart cannot diagnose the cause.

Tell the clinician about the dates, amount and duration, whether pregnancy is possible, recent childbirth, medicines and contraception. Any bleeding or blood-stained discharge after menopause needs assessment, even if it happens once or is only a small brown stain.

Check whether a tampon or other item could remain inside

A retained tampon, condom or another vaginal item can cause discharge, odour or irritation. A tampon cannot pass through an intact cervix into the abdomen, but it can sit high in the vagina and be difficult to reach.

If a tampon is easily reachable, you can try removing it gently with clean fingers. Do not use tweezers or other tools, and do not keep trying if it hurts. Seek prompt help if you cannot remove it, are unsure whether something remains, or have pain, odour or discharge.

A retained item does not always cause toxic shock syndrome, but this rare infection can progress quickly. Fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, a widespread rash, dizziness or feeling very unwell while using a tampon or menstrual cup needs urgent medical help. Remove the product if possible without delaying care.

Call emergency services for collapse, confusion, breathing difficulty or rapidly worsening illness. Toxic shock can also occur in other situations, including with infected wounds; it is not diagnosed by the colour of discharge.

Other possible retained items include a contraceptive cap or sponge, part of a sex toy, or a second tampon inserted before the first was removed. Local swelling, itching or difficulty urinating can accompany the discharge. Tell the clinician exactly what may remain rather than trying to retrieve it with an instrument.

Infection may cause bleeding as well as discharge

Some vaginal or cervical infections can cause unusual discharge, bleeding after sex or bleeding between periods. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea may have few symptoms, so a lack of pain or odour does not exclude them.

Pelvic inflammatory disease can cause lower abdominal pain, pain during sex, abnormal bleeding or discharge, and sometimes fever. Seek prompt assessment if these symptoms occur, because early treatment reduces the risk of complications.

Testing may include swabs or urine samples and a pregnancy test. Treatment depends on the infection; do not choose an antibiotic or antifungal because discharge looks dark. Partner treatment and avoiding sex for the recommended interval may be part of the plan.

Untreated pelvic infection can contribute to chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy or fertility problems. Complete prescribed treatment and follow partner-testing advice; do not assume symptoms disappearing means a bacterial STI has been cleared.

If pregnancy is possible, colour cannot provide reassurance

Take a pregnancy test at an appropriate time if your period is late or pregnancy is possible. A test taken too early may be negative, so follow the instructions and repeat it when advised.

Report bleeding or brown discharge in a known pregnancy to your maternity or early-pregnancy service. Light spotting can have several causes. You cannot reliably identify “implantation bleeding” by its colour, date or duration, and it should not be used to dismiss a new symptom.

An ectopic pregnancy can cause light or dark bleeding rather than a heavy red flow. Get urgent assessment for bleeding with pelvic pain when pregnancy is possible, even without a positive home test. Severe or one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting or marked dizziness needs emergency help.

A missed miscarriage may have few symptoms and be found on ultrasound. Dark discharge does not confirm it, and there is no requirement that pregnancy tissue remain for four weeks before that term applies. Diagnosis may require repeat assessment when a scan is too early to be conclusive.

A missed period, tiredness, nausea, breast tenderness or more frequent urination can occur in early pregnancy, but none confirms pregnancy or identifies why bleeding happened. Miscarriage is commonest in early pregnancy; cramps or weakness may accompany it, and some losses cause no obvious symptoms. Testing and follow-up matter more than guessing from a colour or a percentage.

After birth, watch the amount and how you feel

Postnatal discharge, called lochia, begins after birth and can continue for several weeks. It generally becomes lighter and changes from red towards brown or pink, then paler discharge. The course varies, so one exact day-by-day colour schedule is not a safety test.

Contact your maternity team promptly for increasing bleeding, a bad smell, fever or worsening pelvic pain. Do not assume very dark discharge is normal simply because lochia can contain older blood.

Seek urgent medical care if you soak through one or more pads in an hour, pass clots larger than an egg or pass tissue. Sudden heavy bleeding with faintness, a racing heartbeat or shortness of breath needs emergency help. Do not wait to meet a clot-size threshold if you feel unwell.

Less common causes need an examination

An obstruction can occasionally prevent menstrual blood from leaving normally, especially in a young person with recurring pain but no expected periods. Blood collected in the vagina is called haematocolpos. This is different from amenorrhoea, which simply means absent periods and has many possible causes.

Pain, pressure or urinary difficulty with absent periods warrants assessment. A complete obstruction may prevent discharge entirely; a dark stain is not a reliable way to recognise it. Treatment depends on the anatomy and should be planned by an appropriate specialist.

Cancer is one possible cause of unexplained bleeding or blood-stained discharge, but black discharge is not a specific cancer sign. Persistent bleeding after sex, bleeding after menopause or an ongoing unexplained change should be investigated. A previous normal screening result does not replace assessment of new symptoms.

Obstruction can arise from a hymenal opening that did not form, a vaginal septum, or narrowing or absence of part of the cervical outflow route. A congenital missing cervix and acquired cervical scarring are different conditions. Depending on the anatomy, a procedure to create or restore an opening may be needed; it is not something to clear at home.

Symptoms that can accompany cervical cancer include watery or blood-stained discharge, persistent pelvic pain and, in more advanced disease, leg swelling or problems passing urine or stool. Fatigue and unexplained weight loss also warrant review. These are not specific to cancer. If cancer is diagnosed, surgery, radiotherapy and drug treatments are selected according to its stage and other findings.

Treat the cause rather than the colour

An examination may be enough to identify a retained item or irritation; other situations need infection tests, ultrasound or further investigation. Ask what follow-up is needed if the initial result does not explain continuing symptoms.

If miscarriage is confirmed, options may include waiting, medication or a procedure, depending on clinical circumstances and preference. Surgery does not always mean sharp curettage under general anaesthesia; suction procedures and different anaesthetic options may be available.

Avoid douching, deodorants and home remedies intended to remove dark blood. Gentle external washing is enough while you seek advice. Keep track of symptoms, and seek care sooner if the amount increases or you become unwell.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS advises assessment of new abnormal bleeding, pregnancy bleeding and bleeding after menopause; discharge colour does not establish the cause.

Infection, a retained item, obstruction and pregnancy loss require different investigations and treatments.

How BeMama can help

Record the timing, amount, associated symptoms and pregnancy or postpartum context to help decide the appropriate next step.

When to seek help

Heavy bleeding, faintness, severe pain, fever or rapid systemic illness needs urgent care; pregnancy and postpartum warning signs should not be dismissed because blood looks old.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Very dark discharge often contains older blood, but colour is not a diagnosis.
  • New bleeding between periods, after sex or after menopause needs review.
  • Possible retained items should be removed safely and promptly.
  • Pregnancy-related bleeding needs advice regardless of colour.
  • Heavy bleeding, severe pain, fainting or systemic illness needs urgent care.

Frequently asked questions

Does black discharge mean a miscarriage?

No. Neither miscarriage nor a healthy pregnancy can be confirmed from discharge colour. Pregnancy testing and clinical assessment may be needed.

Can I wait because the blood looks old?

Do not rely on that. Pain, pregnancy, postnatal symptoms, fever, heavy bleeding and bleeding after menopause change what assessment is needed.

Should I wash inside the vagina to clear it?

No. Internal washing can irritate the area and does not treat the underlying cause.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
